title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry | NOEMA
gist: The death of a 4-year-old in a $860,000 patient-funded Shanghai gene-editing trial, plus other undisclosed trial deaths, exposes how China's fast, hospital-approved investigator-initiated trial (IIT) system traded quality control for speed. The new Order 818 tightens rules but lacks reviewer capacity, inspections and whistleblowing, so the author argues investors and regulators should look past China's few biotech successes to a hidden ocean of low-quality trials.

insights.claim: Parents paid Shanghai Jiao Tong University neuroscientist Qiu Zilong's team $860,000 for a customized AAV-delivered brain gene-editing therapy for their 4-year-old daughter Mei, who had a mild genetic condition; she died within days of the March 24, 2025 spinal injection from fever and kidney failure.
insights.speaker: Jane Qiu
insights.so_what: Patient-funded bespoke gene therapy in China can bypass normal risk-benefit gates; AAV high-dose toxicity remains a live safety risk for the gene-editing sector.

insights.claim: China's bioethics history since the late 1980s is a recurring cycle of hype-driven scandals: unproven stem-cell tourism in 2006, bogus immunotherapy ads until the death of Wei Zexi, and He Jiankui's 2018 CRISPR babies, now followed by Mei's death.
insights.speaker: Jane Qiu
insights.so_what: Each new hot modality in China tends to produce a scandal then a regulatory clampdown; anticipate policy shocks following hype cycles.
insights.quote: its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

insights.speaker: Jane Qiu

themes.theme: Dual-track system and the IIT boom

insights.claim: Healthy China 2030 (launched 2016) prioritized rapid clinical application of emerging medical technologies for national competitiveness, creating a health-ministry 'technology track' alongside NMPA drug approval, known as the dual-track regulatory system.
insights.speaker: Jane Qiu
insights.so_what: China's speed advantage in first-in-human biotech is a deliberate industrial-policy choice, competing with Xi's stated 'ethics first' rhetoric.
insights.locator: But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction.

insights.claim: Until new rules took effect in May 2026, Chinese investigator-initiated trials (IITs) could proceed on hospital approval alone without national regulatory oversight, making first-in-human testing faster and cheaper and helping attract investment.
insights.speaker: Jane Qiu
insights.so_what: The cost/speed edge that made China attractive for early-stage biotech data generation is now being curtailed by regulation.
insights.locator: Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated

insights.claim: More than 40,000 investigator-initiated trials had been registered in China by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China's translational research.

insights.claim: China's State Council Order No. 818, effective May 2026, limits IITs to top-tier hospitals, requires health-ministry review for gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies, mandates adverse-event reporting within five working days, and threatens fines, bans, license loss and criminal charges.
